period: The successor balance after Ipsus, 301 BC
background: Antigonus has fallen at Ipsus and his realm is divided among the victors. Seleucus, Lysimachus, Ptolemy and Cassander hold the main kingdoms, while Demetrius survives as a sea power with Cyprus and the Phoenician ports. The opening shows one consistent snapshot, though several holdings were still disputed.
abstractions: Coele-Syria, Lycia, Pamphylia, Caria and Cilicia were contested in 301 BC; the game assigns them to one holder each as a design choice. Antioch (founded about 300 BC) is not present. Seats are grouped polities; borders, forces and populations are designed.
validation: Provisional recommendations: playable IDs, opening city networks, one army per regular seat and starting fleets checked. Human difficulty, balance and mountain-crossing routes have not been playtested for this guidance.

powers.advice: Suggested for the biggest holdings, from Syria to the plateau. Your reach is wide and your armies few: choose a front before the others combine.
Suggested as the default opening: a secure core, a starting fleet and a claim on Coele-Syria. Expanding into the Levant means facing both Demetrius and the Seleucid kingdom.
Suggested for a long chain of cities from the Danube side to the Aegean coast; watch the Straits and the coastal ports that others contest.
A strong European base with Greek neighbours and a fleet. Aetolia, Epirus and Athens are small seats to subdue or ally with.
A fleet-centred position on Cyprus, Tyre, Sidon and Aegean bases with few land connections. Transport is essential, and landing places and supply decide every campaign.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Art of the Hellenistic Age and the Hellenistic Tradition
